1.1: The book opens with King Dhritarashtra asking his minister Sañjaya what happened as his own sons and the sons of Pandu gathered, eager for battle, on the sacred field of Kurukṣetra. Everything that follows — the whole Gītā — is Sañjaya's report back to an anxious father in the palace.
1.2: Sañjaya begins his account. Seeing the Pandava army drawn up for battle, Duryodhana — prince of the Kauravas — walks over to his teacher Droṇa and starts to speak. What follows, through verse 11, is Duryodhana's own assessment of the two armies.
1.3: Duryodhana points out the Pandava army to Droṇa, noting it was arrayed by Dhrishtadyumna, son of King Drupada — who happens to be Droṇa's own former student, now leading the opposing side. A pointed detail to open his speech with.
1.4: Duryodhana starts naming the Pandava side's strength: mighty archers who can match Bhima and Arjuna themselves, including Satyaki, Virata, and Drupada — each a formidable warrior in his own right.
1.5: The roll call continues: Dhrishtaketu, Chekitana, the valiant king of Kashi, Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Shaibya — more names Duryodhana ticks off among the Pandava ranks.
1.6: He finishes the list with Yudhamanyu, Uttamaujas, Abhimanyu (son of Subhadra and Arjuna), and the five sons of Draupadi — all, he says, great chariot-warriors.
1.7: Duryodhana now turns to his own side, asking Droṇa to take note of the leading commanders in his own army. He says he'll name them so Droṇa is reminded who stands with them.
1.8: He names his generals: Droṇa himself, Bhīṣma, Karna, Kripa (undefeated in battle), Ashvatthama, Vikarna, and Bhurishrava, son of Somadatta.
1.9: And many other heroes, he adds, ready to give up their lives for him, skilled with every kind of weapon. One traditional reading hears something telling in this long, reassuring roll call: reciting your own strength at such length can itself betray the fear it's meant to cover.
1.10: Duryodhana sums up: our army, protected by Bhīṣma, is not enough — theirs, protected by Bhima, is enough. The traditions read this differently: Śaṅkara takes it almost the opposite way, that the Kaurava force is the vast, unlimited one and the Pandava force the limited one — the Sanskrit word here genuinely allows both readings.
1.11: So, he orders, let every division commander hold their post and — above all — protect Bhīṣma. One traditional reading finds this telling in itself: insisting so hard on guarding one man can betray an unspoken doubt about how solid that man's loyalty really is.
1.12: Bhīṣma, the aged and revered elder of the Kuru clan, roars like a lion and blows his conch to lift Duryodhana's spirits. Some commentators read this less as a verdict on the coming battle and more as a grandfather's gesture of loyalty to a nephew he privately has doubts about.
1.13: At once, conches, kettledrums, and horns blast out across the Kaurava ranks — an overwhelming wall of sound announcing that battle is near.
1.14: Krishna and Arjuna, seated together in their grand chariot yoked with white horses, answer with conches of their own.
1.15: Krishna blows his conch Panchajanya, Arjuna blows Devadatta, and Bhima — capable of terrible feats — blows the great conch Paundra. Even the instruments carry names here, each one a kind of signature.
1.16: King Yudhishthira blows the Anantavijaya; his younger brothers Nakula and Sahadeva blow the Sughosha and the Manipushpaka.
1.17: More conches sound from the Pandava side: the king of Kashi, the great warrior Shikhandi, Dhrishtadyumna, Virata, and the unconquered Satyaki.
1.18: Drupada, the five sons of Draupadi, and Abhimanyu (son of Subhadra) each blow their own conch too — the Pandava army answering the Kauravas note for note.
1.19: The combined roar is so tremendous it seems to shatter the hearts of Dhritarashtra's men, echoing through sky and earth. Only one side is shaken by the sound — a detail some commentators read as the fragility of a side that already senses it is in the wrong.
1.20: Seeing the Kaurava troops arrayed and battle about to begin, Arjuna — whose banner carries the emblem of Hanuman — raises his bow and turns to speak to Krishna.
1.21: Arjuna asks Krishna, calling him Achyuta ('the unfailing one'), to drive his chariot into the middle — between the two armies. It's the first appearance of a phrase, 'between the two armies,' that recurs through this scene, and again at the exact spot where the Gītā's teaching will begin.
1.22: He explains why: he wants to look over everyone arrayed for battle, to know exactly who he will be fighting in this war before it starts.
1.23: Specifically, he wants to see who has gathered to fight for Duryodhana — whom he already calls 'evil-minded.' That single epithet, dropped before he has seen a single face across the field, already tells us how Arjuna sees the man who brought this war about.
1.24: Sañjaya narrates: at Arjuna's request, Krishna drives the magnificent chariot into the space between the two armies.
1.25: Right in front of Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and all the assembled kings, Krishna says simply: 'Arjuna, look — here are the Kurus, gathered together.' One traditional reading takes this positioning as deliberate on Krishna's part — placing Arjuna exactly where his hidden attachment to his family will surface, because that breakdown is what the teaching to come will need.
1.26: There, Arjuna sees them: fathers, grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, friends — his own extended family, split across both armies and about to fight each other.
1.27: Seeing all these kinsmen arrayed before him, Arjuna is overcome — the text says 'by compassion' — and begins to speak in sorrow. One traditional reading pushes back on that word: what looks like compassion here, it argues, may really be dread wearing compassion's face, since refusing to oppose real wrongdoing isn't the same thing as mercy.
1.28: Arjuna finally speaks: 'Krishna, seeing my own people gathered here, eager to fight—' He can barely get the sentence out before his body starts to fail him.
1.29: His limbs give way, his mouth goes dry, his body trembles, and his hair stands on end — Arjuna describes the physical grip of his own dread.
1.30: The bow Gandiva slips from his hand, his skin burns, he can't stand steady, and his mind seems to spin. The breakdown is total, not just emotional.
1.31: He sees bad omens everywhere, he says, and can foresee no good coming from killing his own kinsmen in this battle.
1.32: He tells Krishna plainly: he wants no victory, no kingdom, no pleasures. What use is any of it — rule, comfort, even life itself?
1.33: Because the very people for whose sake anyone would want a kingdom or its pleasures are the ones standing here, ready to risk their lives and wealth in this fight.
1.34: He lists who they are: teachers, fathers, sons, grandfathers, uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law — kinsmen on every side of him.
1.35: He would not kill them, he says, even if they killed him first — not for rule over three worlds, let alone for this one earth.
1.36: What joy could come from killing Dhritarashtra's sons? Only sin, he says — even though, by the usual reckoning, they are the ones who started the aggression.
1.37: So it isn't right for us to kill them, our own relatives, he concludes. How could we ever be happy again after killing our own kin?
1.38: He allows that Duryodhana's side, blinded by greed, may not see anything wrong in destroying a family or betraying friends.
1.39: But we do see it clearly, he argues — so why shouldn't we, of all people, know to turn away from this sin?
1.40: When a family is destroyed, he reasons, its long-held traditions collapse with it; and when those traditions go, lawlessness takes over everything that's left.
1.41: Once that happens, he continues, the women of the family are corrupted; and once that happens, the boundaries between social classes break down entirely.
1.42: This breakdown, he says, sends both the family and its destroyers to hell, because the ancestors are left without the ritual offerings that once sustained them.
1.43: Through these very failures — the ones causing the breakdown — even a family's oldest, most sacred practices collapse for good.
1.44: 'We have heard,' he says, invoking received wisdom, that people whose family duties have collapsed are bound for hell for an unknown length of time.
1.45: 'Alas,' he says, 'what a terrible sin we're about to commit' — ready to kill our own kinsmen for nothing more than the pleasures of a kingdom.
1.46: He would rather, he says, that Dhritarashtra's armed sons kill him right now, while he stands here unarmed and offering no resistance — the clearest sign yet of how far his despair has gone.
1.47: Sañjaya closes the chapter: having said all this in the middle of the battlefield, Arjuna lets his bow and arrows fall, and sinks down onto the seat of his chariot, his mind overwhelmed with grief. Chapter one ends not with a decision, but with a collapse.
